title: 'Don’t want to spoil the surprise': Rahul on INDIA bloc's next step in CEC-SIR row
text:
NEW DELHI: Congress leader Rahul Gandhi on Tuesday said he does not want to reveal the opposition's next step amid the CEC-SIR row, saying that revealing the strategy would spoil excitement and sense of surprise for the citizens of the country. "Sooner or later, whether tomorrow, the day after, in three months, six months, a year, or two years, it (protests) will not stop. It will reach the end goal. I cannot tell you exactly how we will get there, because that would spoil the surprise, and we want to maintain the excitement and sense of surprise for you and the country," Rahul Gandhi told reporters at a joint briefing of opposition parties at his residence, where he hosted them for evening tea. The Lok Sabha leader of opposition asserted that the Congress-led INDIA bloc would continue its fight against the government with the same energy, strength and unity with which it mobilised for the protests against Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls exercise. title: 'Don’t post videos': Embassy issues fresh advisory for Indians in Saudi
text:
The fresh advisories come after an October 10 attack on Riyadh airport killed an Indian national

NEW DELHI: Indian embassies in Saudi Arabia on Tuesday issued fresh advisories for Indian nationals amid flight disruptions following the suspension of services by Indian airlines to several Saudi cities until October 17. The Indian Embassy in Riyadh advised Indian nationals to remain calm and vigilant, stay indoors in the event of an aerial attack and follow instructions issued by local authorities through official channels. It also urged Indians to refrain from circulating or reposting videos or news related to the ongoing events. The Embassy said Air India and Air India Express had suspended flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam and Jeddah until October 17. Akasa Air suspended services to and from Riyadh and Jeddah, while IndiGo cancelled flights to and from Riyadh, Dammam, Jeddah and Medina until the same date. The General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) has announced the suspension of operations at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh. Operations at other major airports, including Dammam, Jeddah and Medina, are continuing, although disruptions have been reported. The Embassy advised Indian nationals to remain in regular contact with their respective airlines and verify the latest status of their flights. Those needing to leave Saudi Arabia in an emergency may also consider flights from neighbouring Gulf countries, particularly Qatar and Bahrain, subject to obtaining the required visas. The Consulate General of India in Jeddah issued a separate advisory, particularly for Umrah pilgrims travelling to and from Jeddah and Medina. It urged passengers to check with airlines before proceeding to airports and remain in contact with travel agents, tour operators and Umrah service providers regarding cancellations, rescheduling, alternative travel arrangements and accommodation. The Consulate said it was in regular contact with airlines and local authorities to assist affected Indian nationals. Both the Embassy in Riyadh and the Consulate in Jeddah have established 24x7 control rooms to provide assistance. The Riyadh Embassy also said Indian nationals who arrived in Saudi Arabia on visit, tourist, Umrah or business visas but were forced to overstay because of flight unavailability would be allowed to leave without paying fines. Those whose visas have expired were advised to exit the Kingdom as soon as flights become available. title: US issues power grid emergency in 13 states: Reason and what it means for residents
text:
Power plant (Representational image)

US Secretary of Energy Chris Wright has issued an emergency order authorising PJM Interconnection, the regional transmission operator serving much of the Mid-Atlantic and Midwest regions, to run designated power generation units as needed to protect grid stability. The federal directive, issued on October 12, grants PJM temporary emergency authority running from October 13 through October 16. Under the order, the grid operator can mandate certain power plants to generate electricity and, in limited circumstances, tap into backup power reserves to maintain a steady flow of energy across its multistate network, as per the order available on the department’s official website. Federal officials and grid managers clarified that the order is designed specifically to prevent power interruptions and not to announce scheduled blackouts.

Why the emergency order has been issued

Headquartered in the Philadelphia area, PJM Interconnection coordinates wholesale electricity movement across all or parts of 13 states and the District of Columbia. “PJM serves as the Reliability Coordinator and Balancing Authority for its region and is, therefore, responsible for overseeing the dispatch of generation to meet system demand at all times within the limits of the transmission system. The PJM Region includes all or parts of Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia, West Virginia, and the District of Columbia,” the order says. Ahead of strained conditions, the operator issued a Maximum Generation Alert and a Load Management Alert for October 13, pointing to a confluence of weather and scheduled infrastructure downtime. Due to ‘unseasonably warm autumn weather’, forecasted electricity demand is expected to reach approximately 111,500 megawatts or higher on October 13. The second reason is the maintenance window. The grid is currently in its standard seasonal outage cycle, which runs from mid-September through early December. During this period, utilities routinely take generation units and power lines offline for maintenance and upgrades to ensure peak availability ahead of freezing winter weather. Scheduled transmission line outages have restricted the volume of electricity that can be transferred between different zones on the system. title: Iran seeking to expand attacks in UK to military sites, MI5 chief warns
text:
File photo: UK's RAF Fairford base

Iran is seeking to expand its attacks in Britain to include military installations, with the suspected plot against the US-run RAF Fairford air base in September being “not unique”, MI5 chief Ken McCallum said on Tuesday. Speaking in his annual assessment of threats to the UK, the head of Britain's domestic security service said Tehran was increasingly looking beyond its traditional targets, including Iranians opposed to the country's Islamic authorities, to strike more difficult targets such as military sites. “The RAF Fairford incident ... is not unique. There have been other examples, not just in the UK but around the world,” McCallum said, according to Reuters. The comments came as British detectives continued investigating the suspected plot against RAF Fairford in western England, which has been used by US bombers to carry out strikes on Iran during this year's war.

Security alert at RAF Fairford

The suspected plot triggered a major security operation on September 27, when scores of residents were evacuated from their homes near the air base as armed police officers and army bomb-disposal experts moved into the area. Police later said they had found a quantity of gasoline, described as an accelerant, in three vans at the site. No explosives were found. British authorities have linked Tehran to the incident, which prompted the US to withdraw its bombers from RAF Fairford. Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Monday that the suspected plot was “almost certainly” directed by Iran's Revolutionary Guard. Earlier, he said that Tehran was “highly likely” to have been behind the suspected plot. Seven men in their 20s have been arrested and released on bail under investigation. McCallum said he could not comment on the Fairford incident because the investigation was ongoing. He nevertheless pointed to a broader shift in Iran's activities. “A major shift this year has been Iranian ambitions to come at harder targets, like military sites,” he said. McCallum also referred to arson and sabotage attacks on Jewish sites in Britain, which the UK has attributed to Iranian proxies. I ran has denied involvement in the suspected Fairford plot, although it has previously said it considers any military base used to attack its territory a legitimate target.

MI5 flags Russia's activities and AI threats

McCallum also warned about Russia's activities against Britain and its allies, describing Moscow as the leading state aggressor, according to Reuters. He said Russia was escalating its use of hybrid warfare against countries supporting Ukraine, employing tactics that fall short of conventional military conflict. He cited an attempted drone attack on a cargo plane at a German airport and a cyber attack on Polish energy infrastructure as examples. “It's no accident that Russian aggressors are trying to unsettle other European homelands at a time when their military progress in Ukraine is minimal and horrifically costly,” McCallum

title: Ashwin reveals what drove Bhuvneshwar's India comeback
text:
Bhuvneshwar Kumar

Ravichandran Ashwin believes Bhuvneshwar Kumar's return to India's T20I setup is a reward for his consistency rather than the result of chasing an international comeback. The veteran pacer earned a recall to the national squad after impressing for Royal Challengers Bengaluru (RCB) in the IPL, with Ashwin crediting his focus on performance for his return. Bhuvneshwar's selection for India's upcoming five-match T20I series against New Zealand, beginning next week, was one of the major talking points following the squad announcement. The right-arm pacer is set to return to international T20 cricket after a gap of four years.

'He has gone on his own journey'

Speaking on his YouTube channel, Ashwin suggested that Bhuvneshwar remained focused on improving his bowling and fulfilling his responsibilities for RCB rather than worrying about a potential India recall. "I have a feeling that Bhuvneshwar Kumar hasn't even thought about a comeback. I think this will be his mantra for success. And when I'm watching him from afar, I have also experienced this myself, he has gone on his own journey," Ashwin said. "He has focused on doing well, bowling well with the new ball and performing for RCB. Whatever he could do, he did it. His recall is the reward for his success. He never chased that reward; he simply did his job and success followed," he added.

Ashwin backs India for 2027 ODI World Cup, picks South Africa as serious contenders

Looking ahead to the 2027 ODI World Cup, Ashwin backed India to challenge for the title but warned that hosts South Africa could pose a significant threat in familiar conditions. Ashwin pointed to India's pace-bowling resources, spin options and batting experience as reasons to believe the team can mount a strong campaign. He particularly highlighted Bumrah's importance, suggesting that the fast bowler could make a major difference if he performs at his best. "India has the ability. If Jasprit Bumrah is firing on all cylinders, he will have a good fast-bowling experience. India has a good spin stock. There, in a lot of grounds, you will get the help of spin. There is experience in batting," he said. However, Ashwin identified South Africa as one of the strongest contenders, citing home advantage, familiarity with local conditions and the experience players have gained through the SA20 league.

title: Delhi man with 14 criminal cases shot dead, CCTV captures killing
text:
The deceased, identified as Mosin Khan, was a resident of Commander Chowk in Vikas Nagar.

NEW DELHI: A man with around 14 criminal cases registered against him was shot dead in a brazen attack captured on CCTV in outer Delhi’s Ranhola area, police said on Tuesday. The footage shows the victim stopping his motorcycle near a house when two motorcycles carrying four assailants suddenly enter the camera frame. The attackers approach the rider, and one of them opens fire from behind. The other assailants also fire multiple shots at the victim before the attack unfolds in full view of the CCTV camera. The deceased, identified as Mosin Khan, was a resident of Commander Chowk in Vikas Nagar and a declared bad character (BC) of Ranhola police station, according to police. Police said they received information around 5.30 pm on October 11 that Khan had been admitted to a hospital with gunshot injuries. He was subsequently declared dead. A case was registered at Ranhola police station, and an investigation was launched. Police said they had identified the suspects and were making efforts to apprehend them. The motive behind the killing and the circumstances leading to the shooting have not yet been established. Further investigation is underway, police said. (With Agency Inputs)

title: Union minister L Murugan writes to PM Modi seeking exit from Union cabinet
text:
L Murugan

NEW DELHI: Union minister of state for Information and Broadcasting L Murugan has sought to step down from the Union Council of Ministers and relinquish his Rajya Sabha membership, saying he wants to return to grassroots politics. Murugan said he intends to devote himself full-time to strengthening the BJP in Tamil Nadu and preparing the party for the 2029 Lok Sabha elections. In a letter addressed to Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Murugan said he wished to focus on expanding the party’s presence across the state. He also shared the letter on X, reiterating his commitment to working with party workers. “With humility and a grateful heart, I therefore request you to relieve me of my responsibilities as Minister of State and permit me to relinquish my membership of the Rajya Sabha, so that I may dedicate myself full-time to strengthening the party in Tamil Nadu,” Murugan wrote in the letter. He added, “I want to go to every village and every street, meet our people, stand beside our karyakartas and help expand the party's presence in every part of the State.” In his post on X, Murugan said, “It has been the greatest honour of my life to serve Bharat Mata and Tamil Nadu under the leadership of Prime Minister Modi.” “Now, I wish to return to the grassroots, stand with our karyakartas and dedicate myself full-time to strengthening the BJP in Tamil Nadu ahead of the 2029 Lok Sabha elections,” he added. Murugan also expressed gratitude to Modi for giving him the opportunity to serve in the Union government, highlighting his background as the son of daily wage labourers. “I do not come from a political family. I come from a very poor family. My parents, who worked as daily wage labourers and cattle grazers, continue to lead a simple life in Konur village,” he wrote.

title: UK shopper paid £15 for royal family ring; it later sold for £5,500
text:
A shopper who paid £15 for an old ring at a charity shop in Leicester has made thousands of pounds after auction experts linked the item to the British royal family. The rare ring turned out to be a 19th-century gold and enamel mourning ring made to mark the death of Princess Amelia, the youngest daughter of King George III and Queen Charlotte. It was sold at Hansons Auctioneers in Etwall, Derbyshire, where intense bidding from buyers around the world pushed the final price to £5,500. According to Hansons Auctioneers, the buyer spotted the ring among everyday items in a local charity shop without knowing its historical importance. After taking it to experts for an appraisal, specialists identified the detailed gold ring as a rare item from the Regency era.

Hidden high street treasure

Charles Hanson, owner and director of Hansons Auctioneers, described the item as "the most important charity shop find I've heard about in a decade." Details shared by Hansons Auctioneers show that when the owner brought the ring in for a valuation, specialists recognised features linked to royal jewellery made during the reign of King George III. "I was stunned and dazzled," Mr Hanson said in an official announcement published by the auction house. "From a simple box emerged a piece of deeply personal Royal history, commissioned by the Royal family itself to honour a lost loved one. This mourning ring was created to commemorate the life and death of Princess Amelia, and it speaks volumes in its craftsmanship and symbolism."

Poignant piece of royal history

Princess Amelia was born on 7 August 1783 and was the youngest of the 15 children of King George III and Queen Charlotte. She was widely reported to be her father's favourite daughter. She died on 2 November 1810, aged 27, after a long battle with tuberculosis. Historical records cited by Hansons Auctioneers state that her death deeply affected the King and played a major role in his final and lasting decline in mental health. According to accounts of her final hours, Princess Amelia pressed a ring containing a lock of her hair into her father's hand as she lay dying. She is said to have whispered the words "remember me". After her funeral at Windsor, her elder brother, the Prince Regent, who later became King George IV, asked court goldsmiths Rundell, Bridge & Rundell to make 52 mourning rings. These were made in her memory and given only to close family members and trusted friends of the royal household. The ring has a crown design above the initial 'A'. It also carries the words "Remember me" in white enamel. "The white enamel used in the ring denotes that Amelia was unmarried at the time of her death," Mr Hanson explained. "White enamel symbolised purity and innocence in mourning jewellery, particularly for those who died young or unmarried. It contrasts with the more commonly used black enamel, which signified general mourning."

text:
The property’s sale comes amid a more measured Los Angeles housing market, where increased listings have given buyers greater choice and reduced the urgency that characterised earlier years. Images Courtesy: Wikipedia and Google Maps

Some houses are built to impress, while others tell a story that unfolds room by room. In Los Angeles, a Spanish-style bungalow once owned by Back to the Future star Christopher Lloyd belongs firmly to the latter category. Blending Mediterranean influences, playful architectural details and traces of Hollywood history, the property has evolved from a modest 1920s residence into an unconventional compound. Artist Diva Zappa bought the home for $2.55 million in 2022 and undertook an extensive restoration before selling it for $2.82 million after just 12 days on the market, states an online report by Homes.

A bungalow with a Hollywood past

According to Home, when Lloyd acquired the property in the 1980s, the original Spanish bungalow was a relatively modest two-bedroom, two-bathroom home. With architect Robert DeYoung, the actor expanded it into a more elaborate estate, adding a one-bedroom, one-bathroom guesthouse and transforming the outdoor space with a swimming pool and extensive hardscaping. The result was a distinctive mix of architectural influences, with adobe-inspired elements and flowing lines reminiscent of the work of Spanish architect Antoni Gaudí. Rather than following a single design language, the property embraced an eclectic character that reflected Lloyd’s creativity and sense of humour. Some of its most unusual details were personal. According to Homes, a mould of the actor’s face adorned the exterior of the guesthouse, while a light switch incorporated a prop from the Jules Verne Time Train featured in Back to the Future Part III. These touches gave the residence a personality rarely found in conventional luxury real estate. Across the main house and guesthouse, the compound offers more than 3,400 square feet of living space, adds the online report.

An artist’s approach to restoration

When Zappa discovered the property in 2022, its individuality remained intact, but years of insufficient maintenance had left it in need of considerable work. The artist saw potential in its unconventional design and took on the challenge of restoring it without erasing its history. Between 2023 and 2025, the renovation involved substantial structural and cosmetic improvements. New roofs were installed, countertops replaced and bathrooms renovated. The house was also raised so that a new foundation could be poured, with hand-laid crystals incorporated into the foundation as a personal, symbolic gesture, states the online report. The fireplaces received particular attention. Four were restored, while the fifth was completely replaced. title: Sergey Brin is biggest donor against California wealth tax; could owe $13 billion
text:
Google cofounder Sergey Brin has emerged as the biggest donor opposing California’s proposed billionaire wealth tax, contribution $102 million to a political group fighting the measure that could leave him facing tax bill of about $13 billion if approved by voters. The development was reported by Fortune, citing state financial campaign records. As per the campaign fillings, Brin has donated a teal of $102 million to building a Better California, a political action committee campaigning against California’s proposed wealth tax while supporting pro-business, housing and infrastructure policies. The contribution makes him the single largest founder of the anti-tax effort. Opposition groups have collectively raised more than $187 million, compared with roughly $32 million raised by supporters of the measure.

What is California's Proposition 40

Proposition 40 will be on the ballot in November. It would impose a one-time 5% tax on California’s 200 billionaires. Ninety percent of the revenue would go to the state’s health care program. The remaining 10% would go to education, food assistance and administration. With a net worth of nearly $260 billion, Brin could owe about $13 billion if it passes.

Billionaires and Gavin Newsom line up against it

Former Google CEO Eric Schmidt and PayPal cofounder Peter Thiel have also donated to groups opposing the measure. Brin has likened the proposal to the socialist society he left behind. “I fled socialism with my family in 1979,” he told The New York Times in April, adding that he does not want California to end up in the same place. Gov. Gavin Newsom has also come out against the tax. He argues it would erode the state’s tax base and cut revenue for social services. In an interview with Bloomberg Businessweek earlier this year, he said it would reduce investment in education, teachers, librarians, childcare, firefighting and police.

Billionaires already moving

Some of the wealthy are shifting their holdings out of the state. Brin now lists Nevada as his residence, according to state records, and reportedly bought a $51 million home near Miami Beach in March. Larry Page, Google’s other cofounder, has moved several assets out of California. His family office, Koop, was incorporated in Delaware in December 2025. Oceankind, the ocean science nonprofit founded by his wife, Lucy Southworth, was incorporated there around the same time.

Debate over economic impact

Supporters of Proposition 40 argue the tax could generate about $100 billion over five years for state programmes. Opponents counter that it could encourage wealthy residents and businesses to leave California. However, a report cited by Fortune noted that California billionaires collectively paid about $4.1 billion in state income taxes last year, roughly 0.2% of their combined $2 trillion net worth. title: ‘Papa, please save me’: Shekhar Suman remembers son Aayush’s final moments at 11
text:
Actor and television presenter Shekhar Suman has revisited one of the most painful chapters of his life, recalling how he continued working while his eldest son, Aayush, battled a terminal illness. In a conversation with The Lallantop, Shekhar spoke about the family’s struggle during the child’s final days, the financial difficulties he faced at the time and the words Aayush spoke shortly before his death at the age of 11. The actor said the loss continues to affect his family, even decades later. For Shekhar, the period was marked by two devastating realities. He had little work and was worried about supporting his family when he learnt that his son was terminally ill. At a time when he felt he had little left to hold on to, he had to keep working while coping with the possibility of losing his child.

Working on a comedy show while fearing the worst

After the call, however, he had to return to performing in a light-hearted comedy show. “I still don’t know how I did it all (continued working),” he recalled, describing the emotional difficulty of switching between his personal crisis and his professional responsibilities. text:
After learning about the proposed sale, the Village of Luckey began considering acquiring the property itself. (AI photo)

Two brothers in Ohio who bought an abandoned, flooded quarry for $330,000 in 2005 and spent 15 years improving it have been caught in a long legal dispute with the village where the property is located. Steve and Tim Snyder had planned to sell the land in 2021, but the Village of Luckey began proceedings to acquire it through eminent domain, a legal power that allows governments to take private property for public use with compensation. The dispute continued for nearly five years before the village abandoned its attempt to acquire the property in April this year. However, the legal battle has left Luckey facing approximately $206,000 in legal fees, with a judgment lien now recorded against the village. According to a report by The Blade, the amount represents nearly one-third of the village's general fund balance of approximately $640,000 at the end of 2025. The payment has not yet been made because the property owners are challenging the settlement agreement reached by their former lawyer. The case began with a failed property auction in September 2021. The brothers alleged that village officials had discouraged potential buyers from bidding, while Luckey maintained that it wanted the quarry as a possible public water source. The disagreement eventually reached the United States Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit, where the brothers' federal constitutional claims were dismissed.

Privacy fears high, but Indians willing to share data

text:
A New York veterans' charity created to offer outdoor retreats for injured service members became a personal source of money for its leaders, state prosecutors allege in a civil lawsuit. The lawsuit filed by the Office of the New York Attorney General claims that Healing for Heroes, A Disabled Veteran's Retreat and Wooded Oasis, Inc., misled local community groups, businesses, and donors. According to the lawsuit, the charity used their donations to pay for personal luxuries and improvements for its founders instead of helping former service members. According to legal filings submitted by the Office of the New York Attorney General, the charity raised nearly $100,000 in donations after launching in 2024. Investigators say almost half of that money went toward personal shopping trips, restaurant meals, vehicle repairs, fuel, and improvements to property owned by the charity's leaders. State officials are asking the court to shut down the organisation, ban its founders from running non-profits in New York, and order them to return the misused money and pay civil penalties.

Private stays and turned-away applicants

The charity operated from a 30-acre wooded property in Bemus Point, Chautauqua County. Its official promotional materials said the land would offer a free, peaceful place for wounded former service members to rest and recover. Investigators from the Office of the New York Attorney General found that the non-profit held just four retreats in 2024 and 2025. All four events were attended only by board members, their relatives, and close personal friends. This meant donated money was effectively used to pay for private family holidays. When disabled veterans with no personal ties to the charity's leaders asked about booking stays, the organisation turned them away before they could even apply. Court documents say the charity's leaders later claimed they could not afford to host full weekend retreats. Instead of offering stays lasting several days, the organisation held short gatherings with food donated by local businesses. These events included activities called "Free Pizza & Fire Night" and "Coffee and Donuts." Each gathering lasted only a few hours and cost the organisation almost nothing.

Unreported income and personal accounts

Along with collecting donations, Board President Thomas Nelsen and Board Secretary and Treasurer Jennifer Milchanoski-Nelsen rented out the 30-acre property in Bemus Point through Airbnb at least 32 times in 2024 and 2025. text:
A controversial research trial that will withhold hepatitis B vaccines from some African newborns was given approval to move forward this week.

It is a central part of the vaccine vision for Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) and a longtime vaccine opponent.

At an anti-vaccine conference last month, Kennedy praised the Danish researchers behind the trial and touted US-supported research on hepatitis B in newborns as exemplifying the Trump administration’s agenda for vaccines, which has included slashing vaccine recommendations and casting doubt on the safety and effectiveness of shots.

Kennedy “wants to make it so we don’t use a birth dose here in this country,” said Paul Offit, an infectious disease physician at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. “That’s the goal.”

Kennedy would never be able to do the trial in the US because of its significant ethical concerns, Offit added. “He’s taking advantage of a developing country … Is it because children in Africa are more expendable than children here?”

Danish researchers plan to enroll 14,000 infants in Guinea-Bissau in the trial, giving the hepatitis B vaccine to half of the babies at birth and withholding it from the others for the first six weeks of life.

An ethics committee at the researchers’ home institution of the University of Southern Denmark voted this week to proceed with the trial, and officials in Guinea-Bissau have also greenlit the project, which the health minister, Quinhin Nantote, initially said was suspended after international uproar earlier this year.

Stig Børsen Hansen, a founding member who was one of two reviewers who presented the study to the Danish committee, resigned from the group in protest on Friday, citing major ethical issues with the study.

“You are now enrolling newborns in a lottery to test a hypothesis,” Hansen said. The children who are randomly selected not to receive the birth dose of the vaccine, those who “lost the lottery”, face in their earliest days the risk of contracting hepatitis B, which can cause irreversible lifelong damage. “They contract hepatitis B in the context of being part of a research project,” Hansen said, which made their infection happen, in effect, “by design”.

Three other members of the committee have also resigned in protest.

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has reportedly set aside $1.6m in this year’s budget for the project, and it will be matched with private funding from the Pershing Square Foundation, which was co-founded by the billionaire activist Bill Ackman, and the Bluebell Foundation.

The CDC, the Danish researchers, Pershing Square and Nantote have not responded to the Guardian’s questions about this trial.

title: ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international law
text:
The Nobel peace prize has been awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commission that concluded Israel was guilty of genocide in Gaza.

The Norwegian Nobel committee said Pillay, who is serving as a judge at the international court of justice (ICJ), has “shown that legal measures can help prevent acts of war and violence”.

“Navi Pillay’s commitment to universal legal principles and her firm moral compass are constants in a long career,” the committee said, mentioning her early work defending Nelson Mandela under South Africa’s apartheid regime, serving on the international criminal tribunal, and then as the UN high commissioner for human rights, as well as chairing the UN independent international commission of inquiry on the occupied Palestinian territory.

That commission concluded last year that the state of Israel was guilty of genocidal acts in Gaza “with the specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza”, and said the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, its president, Isaac Herzog, and its former defence minister Yoav Gallant had “incited the commission of genocide”.

“It is clear that there is an intent to destroy the Palestinians in Gaza through acts that meet the criteria set forth in the genocide convention,” Pillay said on the publication of the commission’s findings in September last year.

Israel refused to cooperate with the commission, arguing it was biased, and rejected its report as “scandalous”. The Israeli foreign ministry reacted furiously to news of Pillay’s award on Friday.

“If there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner,” the ministry said on X, adding: “Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice.

“Now that the Nobel commission has rewarded the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is certainly applauding from hell.”

In its statement, the Nobel committee said Pillay, 85, had “contributed to strengthen the institutions of international law”.

“Her independence, expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time,” the committee said.

“In awarding this year’s Nobel peace prize, the Norwegian Nobel committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law – national and international – underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently,” its statement said.

title: Isaias strengthens to become first Atlantic hurricane of 2026 season
text:
Isaias has become the first Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season, with wind speeds of 80mph and a minimum pressure of 975mb. It is expected to strengthen to a category 2 hurricane as it approaches the US’s northern Gulf coast on Friday, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).

As a result of the strong El Niño, it has been a notably quiet Atlantic hurricane season. The first hurricane of the season has not formed this late since 8 October 1905, which pre-dates the satellite era (1960s) for tracking hurricanes that has allowed for more non-landfall hurricanes to be discovered.

Isaias is expected to make landfall on Friday evening local time, bringing an estimated 75-150mm (2.9-5.9in) of rainfall across the Gulf coast. There may be up to 250mm in places, with a possibility of flash flooding and isolated river flooding.

The NOAA also said there was increasing likelihood of life-threatening storm surge along portions of the northern Gulf coast and damaging hurricane-force winds over portions of the Florida panhandle, southern Alabama and Mississippi. A hurricane warning has been issued and people have been told to prepare for long power outages and to obey any evacuation orders issued.

In Zimbabwe, a state of disaster was declared in the south-east Masvingo province on Tuesday after a severe hailstorm caused widespread damage to homes and critical infrastructure.

Preliminary assessments found the roofs had been torn off 8,500 homes. A further 15,300 people reported shattered windows, leaving many exposed to the elements as the rainy season begins.

The country’s power infrastructure was badly affected, disrupting drainage and sewerage systems, raising concerns about public health.

In Australia, a rare tornado hit the town of Ulladulla, about 140 miles (230km) south of Sydney, on 3 October. Tornadoes are relatively rare in Australia, where there are about 50 each year. This Ulladulla tornado damaged properties and felled trees.

title: Egyptian journalists plan weekend protest over detention of six colleagues
text:
Egyptian journalists are planning a new protest in Cairo this weekend after six colleagues were charged with terrorism offences amid allegations they had been tortured in police detention.

Last week, Egyptian authorities arrested the journalists, from the independent factchecking and investigative platform Matsadaash, accusing them in a statement of being unlicensed and producing false news on behalf of the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.

The journalists – Abdallah Qadri, Mohamed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Mohamed Adel, Islam Barakat, Mohamed Mahmoud and Omar Helal – were arrested at their homes and in the street by plainclothes officers.

One was charged on Sunday, the other five late on Wednesday. All six have told lawyers they had been tortured and forced to film false confessions, allegations that police deny.

“We were horrified by the news of the torture of our six colleagues,” said Hadeer El-Mahdawy, a journalist on the protest’s organising committee.

In a statement issued on Wednesday evening, the public prosecution said “three journalists who alleged ill-treatment had undergone forensic examinations that found no injuries or signs of violence”.

Another journalist, Rasha Azab, was questioned by the supreme state security prosecution for a post on social media criticising the interior ministry over the arrests. Released on bail, Azab faces charges of using a website to promote ideas advocating terrorist crimes. Her lawyer, Mahienour El-Masry, said prosecutors confronted Azab with 11 identical complaints lodged in different governorates over the post.

Lobna Darwish, of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are representing the six from Matsadaash, said the journalists “had told prosecutors that they were blindfolded and handcuffed for days, beaten and forcibly stripped”. Some were given electric shocks, she said, while journalists also described threats to harm members of their families.

Darwish added that they were forced to read purported confessions from sheets of paper in filmed sessions involving “repeated takes” in front of what she described as “professional filming crews”.

The interior ministry has denied the journalists’ allegations of torture or ill- treatment, saying they were “baseless and an attempt by the detainees to evade the accusations against them”. It described the six as “Muslim Brotherhood elements working for the group”.

For journalists, the arrests and alleged abuse form part of a broader escalation from the Egyptian authorities against independent media, amid poor pay and insecure employment across the profession.

“We are at a very difficult moment on every level,” El-Mahdawy said. “But it is very important that we declare our rejection of what is happening and use every tool we have to protect what remains of this profession, and to defend our colleagues and ourselves.”

title: Scientists discover 180,000 giant tortoises on one Seychelles island
text:
A survey of the world’s largest free-roaming giant tortoise population has discovered that the once endangered species is thriving.

A population of Aldabra giant tortoises lives on an island in Seychelles called Aldabra Atoll.

The most recent survey, led by Seychelles Islands Foundation (SIF) and the University of Exeter, revealed there were approximately 180,000 tortoises living on the island. This is the highest figure ever recorded for the species and far exceeds the human population of Seychelles.

The new figure was obtained by a team who analysed five years of tortoise counts between 2018 and 2022. It is the first update since a widely cited figure of 100,000 tortoises from the late 1990s.

Aldabra Atoll is one of only two places in the world where giant tortoises are found in the wild, with a much smaller population living in the Galápagos.

Dr Frauke Fleischer-Dogley, the CEO of SIF, said: “More than 180,000 giant tortoises roaming freely on our atoll is proof of what long-term commitment to conservation can achieve. This is wonderful news for Seychelles, for the world, and for everyone who has worked to protect Aldabra.”

The study, published in the scientific journal Ecology and Evolution, found that the population was relatively stable for this period, with a best estimate of almost 183,000 adult and sub-adult tortoises.

In the 19th century, exploitation of the animals meant there were fewer than 1,000 Aldabra tortoises left on the island, but a recovery programme led to it becoming a strict nature reserve in 1981 and a Unesco site in 1982.

Researchers are now saying it is one of the greatest conservation success stories of the Indian Ocean, with the new study confirming it. “Aldabra’s giant tortoise monitoring programme is one of the longest running in the region, but the atoll’s dense vegetation makes counting tortoises genuinely difficult in places,” said Dr Nancy Bunbury, one of the study’s co-authors.

“By modelling what we didn’t see, as well as what we did, we’ve produced the most reliable baseline yet for this iconic Seychelles species, establishing a benchmark we can use to track the population for decades to come.”

Despite the good news, the study’s authors say that vigilance is essential. Aldabra’s climate is changing, with longer and more frequent droughts predicted to reduce the shade and food available to tortoises, while rising sea levels threaten low-lying parts of the atoll.

The study authors say invasive mammals remain a threat including feral cats and black rats that prey on tortoise eggs and hatchlings. The planned eradication of these remaining invasive mammals, the authors say, could lift the last barriers to further growth of the population and help it withstand future climate pressures.

title: UK asks Interpol to reject Argentina’s ‘politically motivated’ requests for Falklands oil arrests
text:
Britain has appealed to Interpol to reject Argentina’s requests for the arrest of individuals involved in a large oil project off the Falkland Islands.

With tensions over the sovereignty of the British overseas territory reaching levels not seen since the war with Argentina in 1982, UK officials have sought urgent assurances from the international organisation.

A letter has been sent to Interpol’s headquarters in Lyon arguing that “red notice” requests from Argentina for the arrest of such individuals, including British nationals, should be seen as politically motivated.

It is understood that the UK government is concerned by what sources suggested was an attempt to bully people and companies out of working in the Falklands.

An oil project known as Sea Lion in the north Falklands basin in the south Atlantic has the potential to triple the Falklands’ GDP but Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, has vowed to block it. Argentina’s strategy includes attempts to criminalise those involved in Sea Lion and deter other investors.

In its letter, the UK government has urged Interpol to be cautious in its handling of Argentinian requests for detentions, it is understood.

Andrea Clausen, the chief executive of the Falklands government, confirmed that the use of Interpol by Argentina was a threat but added: “One would hope that Interpol wouldn’t necessarily take action.”

She said: “Certainly those of us who have an interest have had a look at certain sections of Interpol’s constitution to see what we think it could mean.”

It is understood that a response from Interpol to the UK government’s correspondence stated that it would respect article 3 of its constitution, which forbids it from undertaking any intervention or activities of a political character.

Interpol screens red notices, which are requests to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition. If circulated to the enforcement agencies, individual member countries then decide whether to act on the requests. Nearly 20,000 were issued last year.

The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

The intensity of the Argentinian menace relating to the Falklands is at a level that UK officials say has not been seen since the war 44 years ago that followed the invasion ordered by Argentina’s dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri.

The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland islanders.

Argentina continues to claim sovereignty over the 700 islands that make up the Falklands and has dismissed a 2013 referendum in which 99.8% of the islands’ 3,600 residents voted to remain a British territory, with only three votes against.

Despite Interpol’s reassurance about its screening of red notice requests, concerns remain that Argentina could convince the organisation’s member states that its requests are not political but rooted in domestic legislation.

title: How a scandal engulfing Brazil’s top court could return the Bolsonaros to power
text:
Thundering to a crowd of thousands of far-right supporters in São Paulo on 7 September, Brazil’s Independence Day, the senator Flávio Bolsonaro focused less on his opponent in the presidential election, the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, than on someone who is not running at all.

“Whoever votes for Lula is voting for Alexandre de Moraes,” Bolsonaro shouted, referring to the shaven-headed supreme court justice once described as “Voldemort” by Elon Musk.

Although Lula did not appoint Moraes to the court, Bolsonaro’s supporters have linked the two men ever since the judge oversaw the case in which the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, was sentenced to 27 years in prison for attempting a coup.

Now, just days before the election runoff on 25 October, Moraes is once again at the centre of a presidential scandal – one that Lula believes may have helped Flávio Bolsonaro overtake him to emerge as the frontrunner. The justice once hailed as democracy’s “saviour” for containing Jair Bolsonaro may now have helped pave the way for the family’s return to power.

The scandal began with a police investigation, which found that Moraes’s wife’s law firm had a contract worth about £20m with Daniel Vorcaro, the banker accused of orchestrating Brazil’s largest banking fraud. Text messages also emerged suggesting a close relationship between Moraes and Vorcaro, though the judge denies the messages are authentic.

Investigations subsequently revealed that at least four other justices had links to the disgraced banker, meaning half of the court’s 10 current justices have been drawn into the scandal.

The crisis peaked last month with a ferocious exchange of insults between Moraes and another justice during a televised court session. A series of rulings followed in which the pair – as well as other judges aligned with each side – overruled one another, dominating public debate for weeks.

Lula, the day after losing the first round, blamed his poor result in part on having to “carry on his back … the promiscuity” of the supreme court, in what many political observers saw as an attempt by the president to distance himself from the crisis. His campaign coordinator, Edinho Silva, said that, “in the eyes of society … [Lula] paid the price for that institutional damage”.

Although analysts point to a range of reasons for the far right’s lead, from household debt to a simple preference for Flávio Bolsonaro, many agree that the supreme court crisis played a decisive role, particularly among indecisive voters who, with the electorate generally divided between two similarly sized left and right blocs, are the ones who ultimately decide the election.

“These are people who thought that, just as they see congress, the country’s highest court had become corrupt, too. That deepened apathy among some who might otherwise have voted for Lula and fuelled the anti-system sentiment that feeds the far right,” said Camila Rocha, a political scientist who

title: Latin American organised crime ‘may operate in 16 European countries’
text:
A four-month investigation by the Guardian has revealed that the surge in cocaine trafficking to Europe is directly linked to the expanding presence of Latin American criminal networks in Europe, where they have forged close ties with local mafia organisations.

The investigation, utilising databases, police and intelligence agencies, along with interviews with judges, prosecutors and experts from eight countries, shows that cartels and factions from Colombia, Brazil, Ecuador, Venezuela, Mexico and the US are active in at least 12 European countries. Between 2014 and 2024, there was a 471% rise in the quantity of cocaine seized and more local laboratories processing cocaine derivatives were dismantled.

The figure could be even higher, as it includes only groups officially identified in Europe through police operations, transnational investigations and ongoing court cases involving brokers, active members, cells or operational networks. It does not include gangs that lack a physical presence in Europe while working in “joint ventures” with European mafias.

The identified groups include Mexico’s Sinaloa cartel and the Jalisco New Generation cartel (CJNG); the Clan del Golfo mafia, and the guerrilla organisations ELN and dissident factions of Farc in Colombia; Brazil’s Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC, or First Capital Command) and Comando Vermelho (CV, or Red Command); Venezuela’s Tren de Aragua; and the US-originated Barrio 18 and MS-13 gangs, which are also prevalent in El Salvador, Honduras, Guatemala and, to a lesser degree, in Mexico.

These organisations have built a more prominent presence in Spain, Portugal, the Netherlands, Belgium and France, while their activities have also been noted in Germany, Romania, Croatia and Slovakia. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (Gi-Toc) also includes Bulgaria.

Daniel Brombacher, a political scientist and director of the Europe Observatory at Gi-Toc, said: “There is something new happening with a presence of Latin American groups in geographies where there’s no pre-existing infrastructure.

“This phenomenon is no longer limited to the traditional gateway countries,” he says. “Recent police operations have uncovered Mexican-run methamphetamine labs in southern France, north-eastern Poland and Brandenburg, south of Berlin. Latin American groups are also appearing in Romania and Bulgaria along the Balkan route.”

Latin American national authorities and experts suggest the list may be even longer. title: Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel kill five people on Mexico’s Pacific coast
text:
At least five people have died after Hurricane Simon and Tropical Storm Rachel pummelled Mexico’s Pacific coast, causing flooding that downed trees and electricity poles, blocked roads and inundated homes.

Simon claimed the life of a 71-year-old man who died when a wall collapsed in Chilpancingo in the southern state of Guerrero, governor Evelyn Salgado said at a press conference.

The storm also damaged infrastructure and homes in the state’s coastal towns, including the major seaport of Acapulco, she said.

Tropical Storm Rachel is blamed for the deaths of four members of one family, including two children, whose bodies were found on the outskirts of the city of Ensenada in Baja California, the state’s prosecutor’s office reported.

Five more people remained missing, while security forces used helicopters to rescue 32 people, prosecutors said. Baja governor Marina del Pilar said officials were helping more than 50 people in temporary shelters.

Simon did not make landfall and, after weakening to category two on the five-point Saffir-Simpson scale, was moving away from the coast, authorities said. A rain alert remained in place.

The National Hurricane Center in Miami said heavy rainfall associated with Simon in west-central Mexico over the next few days might still produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides.

Officials warned waves of up to five metres high were still expected in some coastal areas. Flooding and landslides had already hit communities close to rivers and streams in the states of Michoacan and Colima.

The El Niño phenomenon, characterised by rising water temperatures in the Pacific, is fuelling a more intense hurricanes this season in the region.

Meteorologists say the 2026-27 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niños more intense.

title: Argentina temporarily closes Iguazu Falls after El Niño-fuelled surge in water levels
text:
Heavy rainfall fuelled by a supersized El Niño weather pattern briefly forced Argentinian authorities to close tourist access to the famed Iguazu Falls, amid fears that rapidly rising water levels would cause the river to burst its banks.

National park officials took the precautionary measure on Monday when the Iguazu River’s flow exceeded 12,000 cubic metres per second – more than six times its average rate.

It later said the area would reopen to tourists on Tuesday, citing a “gradual decline” in the river’s flow.

José María Hervás, the director of the Iguazu national park, said access was closed because “it just keeps raining” and the volume of water being released from dams upstream on the Iguazu River was not falling, reported the Buenos Aires Times.

The Iguazu Falls, recognised by Unesco as one of the world’s largest and most impressive waterfalls, sits on the border of Argenina and Brazil and spans approximately 2,700 metres.

In 2023 and 2024, Argentinian officials closed the park on its side of the border over flooding caused by a previous El Niño cycle.

Meteorologists say the 2026-2027 El Niño, which causes global changes in winds and rainfall as well as erratic weather conditions, is certain to be the biggest ever recorded. Scientists now also think human-caused global heating is making El Niño’s more intense.

El Niño begins in the equatorial Pacific where changes in winds allow huge amounts of heat to escape the oceans and heat the atmosphere. It grows in the northern hemisphere autumn and peaks in December but has impacts well into the following year.

Last month, Argentina’s coastal region experienced above-average rainfall “similar to that seen during strong El Niño events,” the national meteorological service said.

title: Indonesia wildfire fuelled by El Niño razes almost 300 homes
text:
A forest fire on Indonesia’s Sumatra island fuelled by El Niño has razed nearly 300 homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate, an official said on Tuesday as the country battles devastating blazes and haze.

Residents first spotted the fire approaching their village in Bangka Belitung province on Saturday and tried to put it out themselves with portable water pumps, said the head of South Bangka regency, Riza Herdavid.

“They thought it was taken care of. But it’s peatland, and there was still a fire smouldering underneath. So, when they assumed it was over, the wind shifted and quickly drove the fire toward the settlement.”

The local disaster agency said nearly 1,000 people had fled the village.

“My house is gone,” said Leni, a 55-year-old woman staying at a shelter with her family.

“There’s nothing left. I could only save myself and take my kids with me ... I panicked and didn’t have the time to grab anything.”

Another survivor, Haryanti, 50, said strong winds had fuelled the flames, which had torn through homes that were made mostly of wood.

“I immediately ran to save myself. None of my belongings survived ... only the clothes on my back,” she said.

Riza said the village had been built on what used to be peatland in a protected area, but which was converted into a housing complex last year.

Indonesia regularly has wildfires during the dry season, but they have been more intense this year because of the El Niño weather phenomenon, which is forecast to be one of the strongest since comparable records began four decades ago.

Experts also point to slash-and-burn land clearances that have changed the naturally fire-resistant landscape of Sumatra and Borneo islands.

This year’s fires have created severe haze locally, with tens of thousands of cases of respiratory illnesses, and caused air pollution spikes in Singapore and Malaysia.

Thick smoke in a province of Borneo has also grounded water-bombing aircraft, according to the disaster agency.

Indonesia’s president, Prabowo Subianto, ordered the government on Monday to mobilise maximum efforts to extinguish wildfires that have been raging for three months in some places.

The cabinet secretary, Teddy Indra Wijaya, said the government had deployed more than 60,000 personnel on the ground.

title: EU to limit Chinese hybrid vehicle imports to 350,000 a year
text:
The EU is to limit the number of hybrid electric vehicles imported from China to 350,000 cars a year, the European Commission has confirmed.

Imports have been soaring in the past two years; about 800,000 battery and plug-in hybrids are likely to be sold this year.

The EU expects that the quota, which will come into force in December, will halve China’s market share, which now stands at 6% in a landmark four-year agreement made in Beijing last week.

The annual limit on imports of hybrids will be taken under the World Trade Organization safeguard measures, which mean it can be implemented swiftly without the type of investigations needed in anti-dumping measures.

Any cars imported above the quota level will not be subject to tariffs, but will remain blocked in customs at docks in Europe.

Chinese vehicles assembled within the EU, such as those made in Hungary or, in future, Spain, will not be subject to the quota, officials have confirmed, but EU companies making cars in China will.

China’s exports of hybrids to the EU tripled to €6.7bn (£5.7bn) in the first half of this year, from €2.2bn a year earlier, according to Chinese customs data.

As part of the deal, China has also agreed to drop some tariffs on auto parts and cut duties by half on footwear, olive oil and ice-cream from the EU.

Officials stressed that the quota is fully supported by China, and further dialogue on cars and other imports including chemicals, renewable energy and furniture is continuing.

“We will continue the dialogue on some products … this is by no means the end of the story,” an official said.

Last month, the EU called for feedback on a new rule that could oblige companies to diversify their supply chains while the“Made in Europe” legislation would do the same in public procurement.

On Thursday, EU leaders will discuss a French-German proposal for a “kill switch” or new instrument that would allow Brussels to block access to the single market for certain goods in the event of any harmful development, such as a ban on rare earths crucial for the tech and automotive industries.

The deal on hybrid EVs comes amid mounting concern over the £1bn-a-day trade deficit the EU is now running with China.

Up until recently, the EU’s strategy for tackling what it says is an “unsustainable” trade imbalance has been to seek to increase exports to China.

Sources said there has been “a paradigm shift” with concerns of deindustrialisation and job losses in the industrial heartlands forcing a renewed focus on curbing imports rather than increasing exports.

“We are closely surveilling, our imports. We know what’s coming in. We know where there’s a surge, and we know what hits the hardest in terms of our deindustrialisation,” said an official.

title: Volkswagen boss backs EU plan to bolster domestic European industry
text:
The boss of Volkswagen has backed EU proposals to boost its domestic industry, arguing European carmakers need to be able to “compete under comparable conditions” with Chinese rivals.

Oliver Blume said “Made in Europe” rules from the EU “must reward real value creation in Europe”, speaking in Paris before the motor show this week.

The rules are aimed at countering the rapid rise of Chinese brands in Europe in the automotive sector and other important manufacturing industries. Lower-priced Chinese manufacturers have prompted a crisis in several industries.

Volkswagen is among the most-affected European companies. Germany’s biggest carmaker has launched a brutal plan to cut as many as 100,000 jobs. Blume said it was the “largest transformation programme in its history”.

The proposals for the Made in Europe rules, formally known as the Industrial Accelerator Act, would limit subsidies and public procurement to products with a large proportion of their materials and manufacturing coming from within the EU.

Blume listed a litany of challenges facing European carmakers, saying: “Europe is under enormous competitive pressure.” These included: high energy costs; lower demand as consumers struggle with high inflation; the need to be quicker to develop cars; and intense competition from China.

On Friday, the EU said it had reached a landmark deal with China to “halve” its sales of hybrid cars in the bloc amid fears surging sales could kill off parts of the European car industry.

Blume said Germany’s carmakers were happy to compete with Chinese rivals, but said the EU should try to reward businesses with significant European footprints.

“Companies that invest and develop in Europe must see a clear benefit,” he said.

Referring to Chinese companies, he added: “Those who sell here should compete under comparable conditions and create jobs and value here in Europe, too.

Blume added: “We believe in open markets, but openness also means standing up for our own interests in Europe. Because a strong industrial base means more than economic success. It protects technological independence.”

Volkswagen is exhibiting at the Paris show for the first time in 20 years. Blume emphasised the “close ties between France and Germany”, while hosting the French industry minister, Sébastian Martin.

Arno Antlitz, VW’s chief financial officer, said the job cuts were necessary to “increase our economic power” by increasing profitability and allowing it to defend its “home turf”.

The company is cutting the number of models it offers worldwide from 150 to 75 across brands including Audi and Škoda. It hopes the move will reduce complexity in its factories and for dealers, cutting the cost of each vehicle it makes.

On Sunday, it revealed the production version of its ID Tiguan, an electric edition of its bestselling family SUV.

title: Cop31 host urges wealthy countries to spend ‘much more’ on climate than defence
text:
Wealthy countries should spend far more on dealing with the climate crisis than the 5% of GDP promised by Nato members for defence because “the climate issue is the security issue”, the host of the next UN summit has said.

But, in comments that are likely to prove contentious, the Cop31 president-designate, Murat Kurum, hedged on whether countries should try to repeat a previous agreement to “transition away from fossil fuels” – the primary cause of the climate crisis – when they meet in Turkey next month.

Kurum, the Turkish climate change minister, told the Guardian the world was “already in a transition” and suggested fossil fuel use could be addressed indirectly through other steps.

Kurum was among national leaders and ministers, officials and civil society members in Fiji this week to prepare for Cop31, which will take place in the Turkish city of Antalya in November. Australia, which has the new role of “president of negotiations” at Cop31, had pushed to hold the pre-Cop meeting in the Pacific to bring attention to island nations.

Geopolitical turmoil from war, a historic energy crisis and an unpredictable and climate-denying US administration – combined with the knowledge that many would be attending the main climate summit in a few weeks – meant only 13 national leaders joined Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in the Fijian city of Nadi, and most were from the Pacific.

But there were also about 30 ministers, including from India and European nations, representatives from the big emitters China and Saudi Arabia, the heads of global agencies and about 4,000 other attenders.

On Tuesday, a delegation flew north to see Tuvalu, a low-lying atoll country of about 10,000 people that is among the most at risk from the climate crisis. They were shown a 20-hectare (49-acre) land reclamation project and heard stories of life in a country that is mostly only about 2 metres above sea level, and where rising waters, storm surges and intensifying extreme weather pose an accelerating threat to survival.

In a powerful speech, Melelusi Sokotia, 13, told the visitors her friends’ dreams to be “teachers, doctors, builders” were being subsumed by the question of whether they could “grow safely here in Tuvalu”.

Back in Nadi, Fiji’s climate minister, Lynda Tabuya, was moved to tears and received a standing ovation during her closing address. She urged delegates to “remember the people you met” and “carry something of the Pacific with you”.

Tabuya said: “This pre-Cop draws to a close tonight. Our responsibility does not.”

The governments of about 190 countries will head to Antalya with clear evidence that responsibility is not being met. title: Sydney trader sacked for working from Singapore without permission wins unfair dismissal case
text:
A Sydney currency trader who was sacked for working from Singapore without approval has won an unfair dismissal case, but failed to be awarded compensation.

The Fair Work Commission ruled on Wednesday that Charles Graham had been unfairly dismissed by HIFX Australia, trading as Xe, in December last year.

Graham was sacked after his manager asked an IT worker to use his “FBI skills” and track the IP address on Graham’s laptop.

They discovered he was working from Singapore. It was also later discovered he had previously worked from Bali after telling his manager he was working from home because he had a plumber “coming around to sort out some recurring bathroom issues”.

Graham was sacked as Xe found he knew he had to get prior approval to work overseas and was to attend the office three times a week.

He said he had been holidaying in Singapore before his partner became ill with a bacterial infection, preventing him from returning to Australia.

He provided documentation, which he said showed his partner required medical treatment.

Graham had previously asked Xe if he could relocate to Singapore, but his request was denied.

Fair Work Commission commissioner Alana Matheson said that after the company sent an email to Graham advising him of its discovery on 17 November last year, the “tone … had clearly pivoted” by the following day, when he was told “there was a case to answer regarding alleged breaches of company policy”.

Over the following 10 days, a series of further email exchanges and a discussion between Xe managers took place.

Graham said in his written response to Xe that he travelled to Singapore for a holiday and that there was no relation to his previous request to relocate there, that the decision to reschedule the return flight to Australia was made over a weekend, and that as there was no expectation or precedent that he contacted his manager outside business hours, he could not inform them of this.

He said that when he did log on from Singapore rather than in Australia “he was bombarded with triaging hundreds of unread emails from his time off, fielding inbound calls and dealing with an eligible complaint from a high-value client”, and this took priority over telling his manager he was stuck overseas.

Among his other responses was that he only intended to spend a short amount of time overseas, he had not been told about specific policies regarding hybrid work, and that he had intended to let his manager know he was overseas as soon as practicable.

title: Anne Aly reveals she has received 19 death threats in the last week alone
text:
Anne Aly has condemned as “racist” and “misogynistic” comments in parliament calling for her to be “stoned in the square” – while revealing she has received 19 death threats in the last week alone.

The Gold Coast Liberal National MP Angie Bell, the member for Moncrieff, told the House of Representatives that Aly, the small business minister, and the prime minister should be “shamed and stoned in the square” over a decision made by the tax office.

Bell was forced to withdraw the comment by the speaker.

On Instagram, Aly responded with an emotive post-to-camera, saying she had been the subject of consistent death threats, including previous threats that she should be stoned.

“I don’t usually comment about these sorts of things, but I feel like I have to. This past week alone, I’ve had 19 death threats on my social media. And in the past I’ve had death threats that are couched in that exact same language: stone her.”

Aly said that the comments directed at her were not just unparliamentary, but fundamentally inimical to Australian values.

Australia – like other liberal democracies – has experienced a dramatic rise in threats against politicians and other public figures.

title: Child safety staff determined to send Elizabeth Struhs home with parents despite doctors’ concerns, inquest hears
text:
It was impossible to change the mind of child safety staff after they had decided to send Elizabeth Struhs home with her parents despite some of her doctors’ concerns, a police officer has told a coronial inquest into the young girl’s death.

Child safety staff decided in 2019 that it would be “more detrimental” to not return Elizabeth, aged six at the time, to her Toowoomba home upon her discharge from hospital after suffering a coma due to diabetic ketoacidosis, a Queensland coroner heard.

Elizabeth died at home on 7 January 2022 after her parents withdrew the insulin she needed to survive type 1 diabetes. Her parents were members of a religious sect known as the Saints. The sect did not believe in medicine, and believed Elizabeth would be miraculously healed of her illness or raised from the dead, the inquest heard.

All 14 adult members of the sect were convicted of Elizabeth’s manslaughter last year, including her father, Jason Struhs, and mother, Kerrie Struhs.

The coroner, Ainslie Kirkegaard, heard evidence on Monday from senior doctors at the Queensland children’s hospital who had repeatedly raised the alarm after Elizabeth was hospitalised in a 2019 incident.

Kerrie Struhs told the authorities at the time that she didn’t believe in medicine, and had discouraged Elizabeth’s father from seeking medical assistance and to instead trust in prayer, the coroner heard.

Both parents were convicted of not providing the necessaries of life to Elizabeth as a result of the incident, and Kerrie was jailed.

After Elizabeth was admitted to hospital in 2019, doctors warned that Kerrie might “sabotage” her long-term treatment for the incurable illness, which requires multiple insulin injections a day, if they lived together, the coroner heard.

But the court heard that child safety officers determined she should be returned home to the care of Jason.

The coroner heard evidence about a meeting held by the suspected child abuse and neglect team in which the decision was made. It was led by child safety officers, but involved specialist police and health staff.

Jason was deemed to be able to provide treatment for Elizabeth, such as insulin injections, the court heard.

According to minutes from the meeting, a child safety officer said: “The Queensland children’s hospital is not agreeing with our assessment and have been very vocal about it. I feel that removing her would be more detrimental and we currently have the father stepping up.”

“I was never going to change their mind regardless of what I said.”

title: The return of the prodigal son? Why speculation is rising over Josh Frydenberg’s future
text:
A reasonable query for Liberals at this point is: if Josh Frydenberg is the answer, what is the question?

There was a whiff of weariness in some corners of parliament this week, as the former treasurer and deputy Liberal leader happily stoked another round of “Josh for Canberra” speculation. With more rumoured comebacks than Oasis, Frydenberg’s latest foray into the national political arena saw him bouncing around TV, radio and podcast interviews to promote his new book, and pointedly refuse to rule out trying to rejoin the parliament.

His book – part family history, part treatise on antisemitism and social cohesion, part political manifesto – is titled A Grateful Son. But is he instead the prodigal son? The one who set out on his own but is destined to be welcomed back to the Liberal party family with joy and celebrations?

Frydenberg is young enough, bright enough and certainly energetic enough to still make a difference in public life. His addition to what is often a tired Coalition party room would certainly spice things up, and give a new weapon in its arsenal. The ideas in his book – a remix of the GST to fund income tax cuts, concerns about the future of his party, changes to the system of federalism, yet more calls for civic service for school leavers – are politically inconvenient for the federal Coalition as well as the Victorian Liberals headed for an election win, but are worth considering.

The talk around parliament is that Frydenberg is privately telling people he is unlikely to seek a return. But the fact he has pointedly refused to rule it out in a conga line of media interviews, saying only that he would make his mind up later, seems opportunistic. The spectre of a potential leadership alternative is hardly a help for Angus Taylor.

Labor sources have helpfully shared key quotes from Frydenberg’s book and media tour, pointing out his calls for changes to GST and the labour market, and criticisms of the Liberal trajectory – again, none helpful to the leader.
