"Get out of the car!" screams a woman, accusing a driver of exposing himself and making obscene comments as she walked by. She is filming the scene in a busy Baghdad street on her phone, and the camera captures him resisting her attempts to open the door as she confronts him.

The video can be seen, with others like it, on the Instagram page of Iraqi women's rights activist Sarah Jassim. She posts them on behalf of women who complain about sexual abuse and harassment by Iraqi men and boys.

"Your camera is your weapon," she tells the BBC. "It's a way to document evidence in case a woman decides to sue her harasser, or at least it is a means to shame him."

One of the videos she posted led to the arrest of the alleged perpetrator, a policeman accused of harassing schoolgirls, she says.

Jassim says posting the videos is risky both for herself and for the women concerned. We have spoken to numerous victims of sexual abuse in Iraq who say that society often blames the victim.

"I have received death threats, and I have also been threatened with acid attacks," Jassim says. "I have been accused of inciting public indecency, because I encourage women to speak in a society that expects us to be silent."

She now barely leaves home, for her own safety, and instead spends hours playing with her dog.

There is a need for stricter laws, she argues, including laws that explicitly criminalise "harassment" and "gender-based violence" - terms that are currently absent from the penal code.

"Recognising the problem is the best way to address it," she says. "We need protection, abusers have to be deterred."

Many Iraqi women have told the BBC they felt failed by the justice and police systems. Pursuing legal action against a harasser or a rapist is a long path in Iraq, with complicated procedures, and uncertain results, according to a number of activists and lawyers we have spoken to.

Violence against women and girls in Iraq is "widespread and under-reported," according to a report in May by a UN committee on discrimination against women, which called for stronger legislation.

Among dozens of recommendations, it urged the authorities to repeal "discriminatory" laws that exonerate rapists if they marry their victims, and allow reduced sentences for murder in cases where a perpetrator was carrying out a so-called "honour killing".

title: Where the US midterm elections will be won and lost
text:
Americans head to the polls on 3 November to decide how the rest of Donald Trump's presidency will play out.

Thousands of races are taking place across the US, at different levels of government. But the main event for voters will be electing members of the House of Representatives and the Senate, the two chambers that make up Congress.

Both of them are currently controlled by the Republicans, the president's party. The success or failure of Trump's final two years in office could rest on the outcome.

Here's our visual guide to where the battle for power will be won and lost - from approval ratings, to key races and issues and the huge amount of money being spent.

One of the reasons the opposition Democrats have a chance to take back Congress is the president's low approval rating, which is a good indicator for how well his party could perform.

He began his second term as president with an approval rating of just over 50%, according to polling resource website Silver Bulletin, but it quickly fell into the 40s.

It was hovering around 42% when Trump decided to launch air strikes with Israel against Iran at the end of February this year but it fell below 40% shortly afterwards. It is currently sitting at about 37%.

Eight years ago, Trump's approval rating was significantly higher at this point in his first term, at 43%. Joe Biden's at the same point in his term was at 40%. In both cases, the sitting president lost control of the House in the midterms but kept hold of the Senate.

But Trump's poor ratings help explain why Democrats are hopeful of winning both chambers of Congress and why they are setting their sights on states that Republicans have won consistently in recent years.

Members of the House serve a two-year term so all 435 seats are up for election in November.

But most districts are not considered competitive because the party that holds them has such solid support that there is only one likely winner.

The Cook Political Report, which analyses campaigns and elections, suggests that just 21 districts are "toss-ups" that could be won by either party.

But winning a majority is no easy task for the Democrats.

They need to keep hold of their seat in Michigan, where polls suggest the race is tighter than Democrats would like between Abdul El-Sayed, a left-wing political outsider, and his Republican rival Mike Rogers, a Trump ally and former FBI agent.

And they would also need to pick up seats in states that Trump won by double-digits in 2024, including Alaska, Iowa and Ohio.

Hundreds of French supermarkets have suffered unprecedented cyberattacks resulting in tonnes of food perishing and raising fears about the vulnerabilities of food systems to advanced technology.

The attacks, which appeared to target internet-linked refrigeration systems manufactured by a Danish company, raised the temperature of fridges and freezers to as high as 50 degrees Celsius (122F) at more than 500 shops and supermarkets across the country. Supermarkets confirmed the attacks on Monday.

The warning comes as the capture of Yemeni territory along the Red Sea coastline last month by the Iran-backed Houthis has raised concerns over the safety of internet cables linking Europe and Asia. title: Rwanda to host a Grand Prix in 2030s as Formula One returns to Africa
text:
Kigali, Rwanda – Formula One will return to Africa after a decades-long absence, with Rwanda scheduled to host a Grand Prix in the early 2030s.

Rwandan President Paul Kagame made the announcement during a ceremony attended by Formula One President and CEO Stefano Domenicali and FIA President Mohammed Ben Sulayem in Kigali on Tuesday.

“Rwanda has been working very hard towards hosting the African Grand Prix,” Kagame said. He referred to it a “partnership” that was long overdue but “a milestone for the continent”.

The East African nation has secured a 10-year deal to bring Formula One back to the continent for the first time since 1993, with the inaugural race projected for the early 2030s.

The Grand Prix will be held near Kigali, with former Austrian motorsport driver Alex Wurz’s racetrack design firm in charge of designing the new circuit.

It will be built near the Bugesera international airport, 40 kilometres (24.8 miles) south of Kigali.

The circuit will stretch over six kilometres, with 17 corners and an anti-clockwise layout. Designed to follow the natural terrain, it will feature an elevation gain of 197 metres per lap. The track will be developed to FIA Grade 1 standards and is expected to host other motorsport competitions and major events.

Kagame emphasised that “Rwanda is happy and excited to be part of a journey that will change how Africa is conceived by the world of sports”.

‘Missing piece’

Mohammed Ben Sulayem, president of the sport’s governing body, hailed Formula One’s return to Africa as “a moment of immense pride”, adding that it opened “a new chapter in the history of Formula One”.

Formula One chief Domenicali termed Africa “the missing piece” in the championship’s global footprint.

In December 2024, the Rwandan president announced the country’s bid to host a Formula One Grand Prix during an address to the FIA General Assembly in Kigali.

Lewis Hamilton, Formula One’s most successful driver with seven world titles and 106 Grand Prix wins, has been a leading proponent of the competition’s return to Africa.

At last week’s Singapore Grand Prix, Hamilton was asked about the prospects of an F1 race in Africa and reiterated his stance, saying: “We need to have a Grand Prix in Africa.”

“It is, for me, the most important continent, to be honest, the most beautiful continent,” the Ferrari driver said. “We’re on all the other continents but that one and there should be no reason for it.”

“He’s flown to Africa so many times over the last couple of years, speaking to lots and lots of different people, so I hope that he has some news for me soon.”

title: African Union holds Kigali talks as fighting continues in eastern DRC
text:
Kigali, Rwanda – The African Union (AU) has held consultations in Kigali, Rwanda, as part of efforts to advance the peace process in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where fighting continues despite diplomatic initiatives to end the conflict.

The consultations, held on October 6, focused on implementing the Washington Peace Agreement, security arrangements, the disarmament, demobilisation and reintegration of fighters, refugee protection and regional economic cooperation, the AU said in a statement.

The delegation comprised former Ethiopian President Sahle-Work Zewde, former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta and former Botswana President Mokgweetsi Masisi. Zewde is the deputy chairperson of the AU Panel of Facilitators for the eastern DRC peace process.

From Goma to Kigali

The Kigali consultations followed meetings in Goma, eastern DRC, on October 5. According to the AU, the delegation met representatives of the United Nations Organization Stabilization Mission in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (MONUSCO), the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the Expanded Joint Verification Mechanism Plus (EJVM+) and the Alliance Fleuve Congo/March 23 Movement (AFC/M23).

Following the Goma meetings, the AU panel called for respect for ceasefire commitments, cooperation with verification mechanisms and restraint from actions that could undermine the peace process. It also stressed the need to protect civilians, ensure safe humanitarian access and prevent sexual and gender-based violence.

In Kigali, the facilitators held separate consultations with Rwandan officials and representatives of regional institutions. The AU said the discussions covered security commitments, the protection of refugees and returnees, and regional economic cooperation, including mineral traceability, cross-border trade, energy and infrastructure.

The facilitators said they would continue their engagements in Kinshasa as part of efforts to support dialogue and advance the peace process.

Two agreements, separate negotiations

The consultations come amid parallel diplomatic efforts to address the conflict. The Washington Peace Agreement, signed by the DRC and Rwanda on June 27, 2025, includes security commitments intended to address concerns over armed groups and the presence of forces in eastern DRC.

title: Australia bowl out South Africa to win first cricket Test in Durban
text:
Australia’s pace bowler Josh Hazlewood has bowled his side to a 214-run ⁠⁠victory over South Africa on the last ⁠⁠day of the first cricket Test match at the Kingsmead Stadium in Durban.

The hosts’ resistance ended before tea on Tuesday as they were dismissed for 206.

Hazlewood took 6-49 ⁠⁠as Australia bagged the six wickets they needed on the last day to go 1-0 up in the three-match series.

He struck twice in one over with the new ball after ⁠⁠already having taken two wickets on Monday and then breaking through South Africa’s stoic early fightback.

The 35-year-old Hazlewood also removed the last batsman to ensure the victory in the first clash between the teams since South Africa upset Australia in last year’s World Test Championship final at ‌‌Lord’s in London.

South Africa held out for the first 110 minutes of Tuesday’s play before a legside delivery from Hazlewood was edged by Wiaan Mulder and snagged by a diving catch from wicketkeeper Alex Carey.

Mulder and Aiden Markram resumed at 102-4 overnight, and the pair extended the fifth-wicket partnership to a patient 69 runs off 205 balls before Hazlewood’s breakthrough, with Mulder making 29.

Part-time spinner Matt Renshaw, who was the man of the match ⁠⁠for Australia with the bat, then took a second Test wicket ⁠⁠when Kyle Verreynne quickly followed Mulder back to the change room with a reckless shot that saw him caught at slip by Steve Smith without scoring.

South Africa were 166-6 at lunch and added 25 runs before the new ⁠⁠ball was taken, but crumbled quickly thereafter.

Marco Jansen was bowled by Hazlewood for 35 and three balls later Simon Harmer followed as he brushed ⁠⁠the ball through to Carey with his glove.

Markram then ⁠⁠fell after a patient 75 off 237 balls, edging Mitch Starc’s delivery off his pads to be caught behind, but was only given out after a television review.

Hazlewood then completed the win as tailender Anrich Nortje popped up the ball ‌‌to short midwicket for Nathan Lyon to catch.

Former Australia captain Smith, who did not field in Monday’s late session after a blow to the head while batting, returned to action on ‌‌Tuesday.

“Steve ‌‌Smith has undergone a series of clinical assessments over the past 24 hours in accordance with Cricket Australia’s concussion protocols and has been cleared to take the field this morning,” a statement said.

Since last week, several student organisations and a wide spectrum of opposition parties have been engaged in a tactical tug-of-war, with tens of thousands turning up on Monday, far outnumbering police personnel.

Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and the resignation of CEC Gyanesh Kumar after revelations of election irregularities. The agitation marks the latest challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s grip on power, after his education minister was forced out by the same group of demonstrators less than three months ago.

The Modi government has tried to portray protesters as representing antinational interests, working to slow down India’s growth or even to enable its breakup.

But India, the world’s most populous country, has had a long history of street protests, from its freedom struggle against the British Empire to waves of movements during the 79 years of the Indian republic that have shaped its modern identity.

“Time and again the government [of the day] has opposed these protests, [and] at times engaged with them critically,” Rasheed Kidwai, a political analyst in New Delhi and former journalist, told Al Jazeera. “But protests have run centrally through India’s story all along.”

Here is a look at major street protests in India and how they often forced powerful governments and leaders to yield.

Anti-Hindi agitations (1965)

India’s newly-formed constitution envisaged Hindi replacing English as the central government’s official language after a 15-year transition, ending on January 26, 1965. Many people in southern India, particularly Tamil speakers in the then Madras state (now Tamil Nadu), feared that this would sideline them in government employment, civil service examinations and dealings with the central administration.

For the federal government of a vast and diverse country, the idea of one common official language of communication was attractive as a tool of unification. Demonstrations by several student organisations, opposing the imposition of Hindi, broke out, often leading to clashes with the police.

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), a regional political party advocating Tamil nationalism, led by CN Annadurai and M Karunanidhi, spearheaded the protests. Students have piled up bins and erected security barriers outside hundreds of schools across the country.

Last Thursday, more than 70,000 people took to the streets in the latest major protest event.

title: Israel and the US see Navi Pillay’s Peace Prize as a verdict on them — rightly so
text:
Advertisement

Israel’s reaction to this year’s prize warrants a return to these examples. “The Nobel Prize committee has lost its moral compass,” PM Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said after the award went to Navi Pillay, a former judge of the International Criminal Court (ICC), “for her efforts to promote peace and international law”. I read the Nobel Committee’s announcement in full. It does not mention Israel by name, and unlike the above-cited dissidents who were targeted by their own governments, Pillay isn’t even Israeli.

What, then, explains the angry reaction from Israel, and from the United States and its president Donald Trump, who claimed to have “never heard” of Pillay? In September 2025, a UN commission that she was chairing at the time concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had “committed genocide” against Palestinians in Gaza. The Committee’s announcement included that commission on Pillay’s list of contributions, and Israel and the US heard the rest for themselves.

Understandably so. By honouring Pillay, the Committee has recognised the validity of an investigation that has placed Israel’s conduct in Gaza under the harshest possible international scrutiny. It has lent legitimacy to the findings that have challenged Israel’s account of its military campaign, which Israel and the US have sought to discredit. And it has affirmed the importance of the institutions and individuals who pursue accountability, even when their findings are unwelcome to powerful states.

Speaking of the powerful, look at Washington’s response. Right after Pillay was honoured, the Trump administration announced new sanctions against the ICC. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US would “ban transactions with this rogue court”. This, despite the fact that the ICC and the UN commission that Pillay chaired are separate institutions, and the Nobel Committee’s announcement does not mention the US at all.

The Israeli-American reaction was always likely to seek to discredit Pillay. But if her career demonstrates anything, it is her relentless pursuit of accountability, most famously in the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda prosecuting those responsible for the 1994 genocide. She is also serving as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the case brought by The Gambia against Myanmar over allegations of genocide against the Rohingya. One can hardly be blamed for putting faith in a woman who has a long record of investigating violence by the state, rather than in a government accused of committing violence and one that has armed and funded it.

And perhaps that is the real measure of the Peace Prize. It cannot compel governments to change course, but it can deny them the final word on their own actions. Thanks to Pillay’s work, the world cannot be prevented from considering the evidence of the destruction of Gaza — however furiously the powerful may object.

title: Can makeup beat facial recognition tech? What Richa Chadha’s ‘tutorial’ gets right, and wrong
text:
From submarines to humans: The CV Dazzle project

The idea of using makeup to beat machines is not new.

In 2010, American artist Adam Harvey’s CV Dazzle (Computer Vision Dazzle) project explored how unconventional makeup and hairstyles could interfere with computer vision algorithms.

“Unlike disruptive-pattern material, CV Dazzle is bright and bold, and evades detection by breaking weaknesses in automated pattern recognition systems,” his website says.

Harvey was inspired by the Dazzle initiative used by the British during World War I, when naval ships were painted in high-contrast colours, and patterns such as stripes and geometric, Cubist-like shapes, to confuse enemy observers about their size, shape, direction and speed. Rather than concealing the ships, the designs were intended to make them harder to track and target.

Story continues below this ad

Harvey’s project, developed as part of his master’s thesis at New York University, did see some success, but facial recognition technology has advanced significantly since then.

How does facial recognition work?

Broadly, facial recognition involves matching a face with one stored in the system database.

But facial recognition systems do not simply compare two photographs pixel by pixel. They use artificial intelligence models to analyse a face and convert its visual characteristics into a numerical representation, often called a face embedding. This is compared with representations stored in a database to determine whether there is a likely match.

The system learns patterns associated with identity from training data. Makeup can alter the image presented to the model, potentially changing the numerical representation enough to prevent a match. This does not necessarily stop the system from detecting that a face is present; it may simply fail to establish whose face it is.

Chadha’s method largely depends on drawing extra eyes and lips to confuse machines, and using colour to alter light and dark patterns of a face.

title: Lesson from IITs: Excellence is nurtured, not inherited
text:

Universities depend on faculty, students, non-teaching staff and members of governing boards. Strong institutions are serious about whom they bring in and continually seek to raise the quality of their people in all these roles. At leading universities, there is often an implicit aspiration that every new faculty appointment should be at least as good as, and preferably better than, the faculty already there. A mediocre appointment can affect an institution for decades. Recruiting outstanding people is only the beginning. A strong institution should enable talented people to become even better over time, expanding their capabilities and ambition rather than allowing them to stagnate.

Universities also need resources: Buildings, hostels, laboratories, libraries, scholarships and research support. These come not only from government grants or tuition fees; alumni, donors and industry relationships are important institutional assets. A strong university will probably never feel that it has enough resources, because greater ambition creates new possibilities and new needs. It must therefore keep building resources and directing them to the right academic priorities.

This is where governance and culture become crucial. Universities need sufficient autonomy for decisions to be taken close to where information and responsibility reside. They need transparent processes, appropriate delegation and clear accountability. Culture is less visible but equally consequential. When people are respected, information is shared, participation is sought and differing views are genuinely considered, they are more likely to feel ownership of the institution. That ownership brings the ideas, energy and passion of faculty, staff and students into building the university.

The IITs benefited from substantial public investment and, compared to typical Indian universities, had a strong resource base. They attracted highly capable students and were exacting in faculty recruitment, with a strong norm that positions need not be filled if suitable candidates were not found. They also enjoyed considerable academic autonomy, with substantial freedom to shape curricula, teaching, faculty recruitment and internal academic practices. Uniformity in curricula, grading or recruitment practices across the IIT system was not the guiding principle; each institution had room to innovate and develop its own identity. This combination helped the IITs build strong institutions. But they are not permanently protected from decline. If recruitment standards weaken, governance deteriorates, culture erodes or autonomy becomes less purposeful, they too can lose ground.

His outlook stands in contrast to warnings from other technology leaders, including Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who have raised concerns about the risks associated with AI.

‘Good thing for society’

Bezos, however, sees the technology as an opportunity to reshape the economy and improve people’s quality of life.

That optimism does not mean he is convinced every company investing in AI will succeed. Asked whether the current AI boom amounts to a bubble, Bezos said it was “hard to know”.

While he believes technology has genuine potential, he acknowledged that the rush to develop and commercialise it has made it difficult to distinguish promising businesses from those unlikely to deliver.

“What I do know is the technology is real. I think this is a good thing for society. It’s tricky for investors. Every experiment gets funded — good ideas and bad ideas. In the moment, in the tussle of this, it’s hard for investors to know the difference between the good ideas and the bad ideas.”

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has suggested that advances in the technology could make a four-day working week possible, and JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has predicted that people might work just three and a half days a week, according to Fortune.

title: Hunter of underwater threats, why INS Mangrol holds importance for the Navy
text:
In total, 16 ASW-SWCs are being constructed together by the CSL and the Garden Reach Shipbuilders and Engineers (GRSE), Kolkata. With over 80% indigenous content, the programme reflects India’s expanding capabilities in naval design, systems integration and defence shipbuilding, the Ministry of Defence has said.

INS Mangrol is named after the coastal town and prominent fishing harbour of Mangrol in Gujarat’s Junagadh district, reflecting the region’s rich maritime heritage. The ship carries forward the legacy of the erstwhile INS Mangrol (M85), a minesweeper that served the Indian Navy from 1983 to 2004.

The crest of INS Mangrol features a Panjmukh, a five-pronged weapon. A social media post about the ship commissioning stated, “Like a Pied Kingfisher, we strike with precision”. The Pied Kingfisher is a striking black-and-white waterbird with a sharply pointed bill and distinctive hovering flight. It is native to the coastal waters of Mangrol.

The features of Mahe class

Built by CSL, the Mahe-class vessels adhere to the classification standards of Det Norske Veritas (DNV), an internationally recognised body that certifies ships against rigorous technical and safety requirements.

They are the Indian Navy’s largest warships to use a diesel engine-waterjet propulsion system, combining improved manoeuvrability with reduced underwater noise. While their primary role is anti-submarine warfare in coastal waters, the vessels are also designed for underwater surveillance, search and rescue (SAR), Low Intensity Maritime Operations (LIMO) and mine-laying. These ships were designed after considering anti-submarine and patrolling operations along the littoral zone.

CSL has stated that each vessel is 78 metres long, has a beam, or maximum width, of 11.36 metres, and a displacement ranging from 896 to 1,100 tonnes. With a maximum speed of 25 knots (about 46 kmph) and the ability to move up to 1,800 nautical miles (approximately 3,333 km) without refuelling, the ships are equipped to operate indigenously developed sonar systems that use sound waves to detect underwater objects.

Their advanced sensors, weapons and communication suites enable the detection, tracking and engagement of underwater threats. The class also features sophisticated machinery, automation and integrated control systems to support sustained operations in shallow waters. Its armament includes torpedoes, multifunctional anti-submarine rockets, and advanced radar and sonar systems.

The need for ships that hunt sub-surface threats

Before the ASW-SWC programme, the Indian Navy relied on four Abhay-class corvettes (which are faster and smaller ships), customised variants of the Soviet-origin Pauk II-class, for coastal patrol and anti-submarine warfare.

After decades of service, these vessels were decommissioned between 2017 and October 2025. To replace the ageing fleet and bolster coastal defence, the Defence Acquisition Council (DAC) approved the procurement of 16 ASW-SWCs in December 2
